claim: Four rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta, 8–13 y old, 10–12 kg) served as subjects in this study.
source: Four adult male rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta, 8–13 y old, 10–12 kg) served as subjects in this study.
evidence: Direct statement in the methods section describing the study subjects.

claim: The four monkeys resided in the same colony room for a minimum of 4 years.
source: These four monkeys have resided in the same colony room for a minimum of 4 y.
evidence: Direct statement about the housing duration of the subjects.

claim: Social behaviors were measured automatically from video using a multi-stage detection based on YOLOv5.
source: These behaviors were measured automatically from video using a multi-stage detection based on YOLOv5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1, see Methods for more details)
evidence: Direct statement describing the methodology for measuring social behaviors.

claim: The YOLOv5 model achieved a mean average precision (mAP) of 0.97 at IoU = 0.5.
source: The mean average precision (mAP) value at IoU = 0.5 is 0.97, and the average of all mAP values, which are calculated by increasing the IoU threshold from 0.5 to 0.95 in steps of 0.05, is 0.89.
evidence: Quantitative performance metric reported for the detection model, shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1f.

claim: Distractor faces significantly impacted the behavioral performance of all four subjects.
source: Distractor faces significantly impacted the behavioral performance of all four subjects, based on paired Student's t-tests across 72 conditions (6 intact faces ×12 experimental days) (Figure 2g, Congruent: MA: p=1.90 × 10–35, MK: p=3.81 × 10–27, ML: p=0.01, MC: p=4.37 × 10–18; Incongruent: MA: p=8.91 × 10–34, MK: p=5.77 × 10–32, ML: p=8.66 × 10–9, MC: p=3.86 × 10–5).
evidence: Statistical analysis with p-values demonstrating significant effects across all subjects.

claim: Distractor biases for individual subjects were negatively correlated with their social engagement indices (SEI(1,1,1)).
source: Intriguingly, the distractor biases for individual subjects were negatively correlated with their social engagement indices (SEI(1,1,1)) with an equal weight of one for all three social relationships (Figure 2j, two-sided Pearson's correlation coefficient, r=–0.87, p=4.51 × 10–88).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with reported r and p values.

claim: Individuals with higher SEIs showed a reduced tendency to be distracted by social information when performing a simple visual orienting task.
source: Specifically, individuals with higher SEIs—that is those monkeys who were overall more social—showed a reduced tendency to be distracted by social information when performing a simple visual orienting task.
evidence: Interpretation of the negative correlation between SEI and distractor bias.

claim: Monkeys spontaneously differentiate between monkeys belonging to their own social group (in-group) and those belonging to other groups (out-group) in the wild.
source: In the wild, monkeys spontaneously differentiate between monkeys belonging to their own social group (in-group) and those belonging to other groups (out-group) (Talbot et al., 2016; Pokorny and de Waal, 2009).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Subjects were familiarized with all distractor images on a daily basis for 8 weeks before the study.
source: Before the study, subjects were familiarized with all distractor images on a daily basis for 8 wk, to rule out any novelty effects.
evidence: Direct statement about experimental procedure to control for novelty.

claim: Response times were faster when monkey faces were illuminated on the same (congruent) side as the target, compared to the scrambled images.
source: Response times were faster when monkey faces were illuminated on the same (congruent) side as the target, compared to the scrambled images (Figure 2e, intact faces: 125.25±48.84ms; scrambled images: 142.80±47.87 ms; Student's t-test, n1=382 trials, n2=372 trials, p=7.87 × 10–7).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test results.

claim: Response times were slower when the target was incongruent with display of a monkey face versus a scrambled version.
source: Conversely, response times were slower when the target was incongruent with display of a monkey face versus a scrambled version (Figure 2f, intact faces: 228.19±30.88 ms; scramble images: 213.97±29.96 ms; Student's t-test, n1=373 trials, n2=385 trials, p=2.17 × 10–10).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test results.

claim: Distractor biases towards in-group monkey faces were significantly smaller than those towards out-group faces, across monkey subjects, on all experimental days.
source: Distractor biases towards in-group monkey faces were significantly smaller than those towards out-group faces, across monkey subjects, on all experimental days (n=4 monkey subjects ×12 experimental days, p=1.45 × 10–7).
evidence: Statistical comparison across all subjects and experimental days.

claim: For 99.30% of the 6561 combinations, distractor biases towards in-group monkey faces were significantly less than those towards out-group faces.
source: As depicted in Figure 3—figure supplement 2c, for 99.30% of the 6561 combinations distractor biases towards in-group monkey faces were significant less than those towards out-group faces (Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, p<0.05).
evidence: Statistical analysis across multiple stimulus combinations to control for specific picture effects.

claim: Attention towards images of both in-group and out-group monkeys was highly correlated with the social engagement scores on three dimensions of social relationships: aggression, grooming and proximity.
source: We found that attention towards images of both in-group and out-group monkeys was highly correlated with the social engagement scores on three dimensions of social relationships: aggression, grooming and proximity (Figure 3—figure supplement 3a–f).
evidence: Statement of correlation findings across multiple behavioral dimensions.

claim: Aggression demonstrated the highest correlation with distractor bias with r values of about –0.8.
source: The correlation coefficients varied across them, with aggression demonstrating the highest correlation with r values of about –0.8.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of correlation coefficients across behavioral dimensions.

claim: The 'best' weights for aggression, grooming, and proximity were 0.34, 0.54, and 0.58, respectively, when monkeys viewed distractors drawn from in-group monkeys.
source: As depicted in Figure 3f and g, the 'best' weights for aggression, grooming, and proximity (ωa, ωg, and ωp) were 0.34, 0.54, and 0.58, respectively, when monkeys viewed distractors drawn from in-group monkeys.
evidence: Quantitative model fitting results for in-group conditions.

claim: The set of 'best' weights were 0.48, 0.62, and 0.92 when monkeys viewed distractors drawn from out-group monkeys.
source: The set of 'best' weights were 0.48, 0.62, and 0.92 when monkeys viewed distractors drawn from out-group monkeys.
evidence: Quantitative model fitting results for out-group conditions.

claim: The impact of social engagement was smaller when monkeys viewed distractors from in-group compared to those from out-group monkeys.
source: The impact of social engagement was smaller when monkeys viewed distractors from in-group (orange lines) compared to those from out-group monkeys (green lines).
evidence: Comparative statement based on analysis of SEI differences.

claim: The average difference of the SEIs dropped significantly from 2.67±1.32 to 1.95±0.99 from out-group to in-group.
source: The average difference of the SEIs dropped significantly from 2.67±1.32–1.95±0.99 from out-group to in-group (paired Student's t-test, p=0.01).
evidence: Quantitative comparison with statistical test.

claim: There was no relationship between the SEIs and performance in visual motor trials without a monkey face distractor.
source: However, there was no relationship between the SEIs and performance in visual motor trials without a monkey face distractor, effectively ruling out any impacts of social tendencies on general oculomotor functions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1d, two-sided Pearson's correlation coefficient, in-group: p=0.08; out-group: p=0.18).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no correlation, serving as a control.

claim: Oxytocin is an endogenous peptide hormone that regulates crucial components of mammalian reproductive systems and influences social behavior more broadly.
source: Oxytocin (OT) is an endogenous peptide hormone that regulates crucial components of mammalian reproductive systems and influences social behavior more broadly (Olff et al., 2013; Jiang and Platt, 2018a; Jiang and Platt, 2018b).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin supported by citations.

claim: Monkeys were administered oxytocin (40 IU/mL, 2 mL) and saline by nebulization for 2 min on alternating days.
source: During the experiment, monkeys were administered oxytocin (40 IU/mL, 2 mL; Beyotime) and saline by nebulization (Omron, infant nebulizer) for 2 min on alternating days.
evidence: Direct description of experimental procedure.

claim: Oxytocin significantly increased distractor bias by enhancing social attention towards out-group monkey faces.
source: Figure 4a shows that oxytocin significantly increased distractor bias by enhancing social attention towards out-group monkey faces (green bars, paired Student's t-test, n=48, p=0.01).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing significant effect of oxytocin.

claim: There was no significant increase in distractor biases towards in-group distractors following oxytocin administration across all individuals and experimental days.
source: Although there was a minor increase in distractor biases towards in-group distractors, this was not statistically significant across all individuals and experimental days (orange bars, p=0.21).
evidence: Statistical test showing no significant effect.

claim: Oxytocin had no impacts on oculomotor behavior during visuo-motor trials without distractors.
source: We found no impacts on oculomotor behavior during visuo-motor trials without distractors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1e, n=48, p=0.31).
evidence: Statistical analysis showing no effect, serving as a control.

claim: There were no significant effects of oxytocin on the probability of first orienting movement towards the distractor between saline and OT averaged across all monkeys.
source: There were also no significant effects on the probability of first orienting movement towards the distractor between saline and OT averaged across all monkeys (Figure 3—figure supplement 1g, n=48, paired Student's t-test, in-group: orange bars, p=0.93; out-group: green bars, p=0.41).
evidence: Statistical comparison showing no significant effects.

claim: The impacts of oxytocin were larger for in-group distractors compared with out-group distractors, with the weight of grooming showing the biggest effect.
source: The impacts of OT were larger for in-group distractors compared with out-group distractors, with the weight of grooming showing the biggest effect (Figure 4f).
evidence: Comparative analysis of oxytocin effects across conditions and behavioral dimensions.

claim: Following the administration of OT, there were significant differences in all 'best' weights on three dimensions of social behavior on social attention to both in-group and out-group faces.
source: We uncovered consistent and significant impacts of all 'best' weights on three dimensions of social behavior on social attention to both in-group faces (Figure 4g) and out-group faces (Figure 4h) (Two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test, n1 = n2=6, p=0.03).
evidence: Statistical test showing significant effects of oxytocin on model weights.

claim: OT reduced the impacts of multi-dimensional social tendencies on social attention.
source: Thus, OT reduced the impacts of multi-dimensional social tendencies on social attention.
evidence: Summary statement based on analysis of SEI differences under oxytocin.

claim: OT most strongly blunted the relationship between grooming and attentional capture by both in-group and out-group faces.
source: Of the three measured dimensions, OT most strongly blunted the relationship between grooming—a prosocial, affiliative behavior—and attentional capture by both in-group and out-group faces.
evidence: Comparative analysis of oxytocin effects across behavioral dimensions.

claim: Individual engagement scores varied with monkeys' social attention, with aggression showing the highest correlation, followed by grooming, and then proximity.
source: Individual engagement scores varied with monkeys' social attention (Figure 3—figure supplement 3g–i), with aggression showing the highest correlation, followed by grooming, and then proximity.
evidence: Comparative analysis of correlations across behavioral dimensions.

claim: Distractor bias and the IEI showed a strong linear correlation (r=0.69).
source: We found that distractor bias and the IEI showed a strong linear correlation (Figure 5d, two-sided Pearson's correlation coefficient, p=2.59 × 10–21, r=0.69).
evidence: Statistical correlation analysis with reported r and p values.

claim: The 'best' weights of ωa, ωg, and ωp with IEIs were 0.54, 0, and 0.04.
source: The 'best' weights of ωa, ωg, and ωp with IEIs were 0.54, 0, and 0.04 (Figure 5c).
evidence: Quantitative model fitting results for IEI.

claim: Amongst all dimensions contributing to IEI, aggression was the most strongly associated with attentional capture by monkey face distractors.
source: Amongst all dimensions contributing to IEI, aggression was the most strongly associated with attentional capture by monkey face distractors.
evidence: Interpretation of model weights showing dominance of aggression.

claim: OT, compared to saline, doubled the weight for aggression in the IEI model.
source: Surprisingly, OT, compared to saline, doubled the weight for aggression (Figure 5g).
evidence: Quantitative comparison of model weights between conditions.

claim: After OT administration, there was a decline in the slope between IEIs and distractor biases from 48.63 (saline) to 23.21 (OT).
source: After OT administration, we observed a decline in the slope between IEIs and distractor biases (Figure 5h, two-sided Pearson's correlation coefficient, saline: p=3.47 × 10–17, r=0.63; OT: p=3.65 × 10–18, r=0.64). Specifically, the slope for saline was 48.63, whereas the slope for OT was 23.21.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of regression slopes with statistical tests.

claim: OT amplifies the impact of dyadic aggressive interactions on social attention.
source: These findings imply that OT amplifies the impact of dyadic aggressive interactions on social attention.
evidence: Interpretation of the increased weight for aggression under oxytocin.

claim: Primates exhibit particularly complex, differentiated, and multidimensional social relationships, which form interwoven social networks.
source: Primates exhibit particularly complex, differentiated, and multidimensional social relationships, which form interwoven social networks, reflecting both individual social tendencies and specific dyadic interactions.
evidence: General statement about primate social behavior, consistent with established knowledge.

claim: Individual differences in social attention vary with individual differences in patterns of general social tendencies and patterns of individual engagement with specific partners.
source: We show that individual differences in social attention vary with individual differences in patterns of general social tendencies and patterns of individual engagement with specific partners.
evidence: Summary statement of main findings from the study.

claim: Oxytocin administration altered social attention and its relationship to both social tendencies and dyadic relationships, particularly grooming and aggression.
source: Oxytocin administration altered social attention and its relationship to both social tendencies and dyadic relationships, particularly grooming and aggression.
evidence: Summary statement of oxytocin effects from the study.

claim: Social relationships bear profound significance for both the development and well-being of individuals within a community and the cohesion and long-term success of their groups.
source: Social relationships bear profound significance for both the development and well-being of individuals within a community (Taborsky and Oliveira, 2012) and the cohesion and long-term success of their groups (Testard et al., 2021; Testard et al., 2024).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Proximity serves as a cornerstone of social interaction, with individuals often seeking closeness to one another for communication, bonding, and safety.
source: Proximity serves as a cornerstone of social interaction, with individuals often seeking closeness to one another for communication, bonding, and safety (Schutte and Light, 1978; Stopczynski et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about proximity behavior supported by citations.

claim: Grooming facilitates hygiene maintenance, parasite removal, and the cultivation and maintenance of social bonds.
source: Grooming is another fundamental behavior for primates, facilitating hygiene maintenance, parasite removal, and the cultivation and maintenance of social bonds (Henazi and Barrett, 1999; Spruijt et al., 1992).
evidence: Statement about grooming behavior supported by citations.

claim: Aggression supports resource competition and the acquisition and maintenance of dominance rank.
source: By contrast with these affiliative interactions, aggression supports resource competition and the acquisition and maintenance of dominance rank (Hobson, 2020; Funkhouser et al., 2018).
evidence: Statement about aggressive behavior supported by citations.

claim: Social networks within primate groups can be characterized at multiple levels or scales, including broader patterns of social tendencies and individual engagement with specific individuals in that group.
source: Social networks within primate groups can be characterized at multiple levels or scales (Aureli and Schino, 2019; Hinde, 1976; Grueter et al., 2012), including broader patterns of social tendencies (e.g. whether a monkey is aloof or highly interactive), as well as individual engagement with specific individuals in that group (e.g. allies, friends, or enemies) (Hobson et al., 2019; Hinde, 1976).
evidence: Statement about social network structure supported by citations.

claim: Primates, including humans, are highly visual animals and actively sample their environments to acquire useful visual information to guide behavioral decisions.
source: Primates, including humans, are highly visual animals (Tsao et al., 2003), and actively sample their environments to acquire useful visual information to guide behavioral decisions (Krajbich and Rangel, 2011; Deaner et al., 2005a; Chang et al., 2013; Chang et al., 2012; Chang et al., 2015; Platt, 2002).
evidence: Statement about primate visual behavior supported by multiple citations.

claim: Both human and nonhuman primates prioritize acquisition of visual social information from birth, orienting preferentially to faces.
source: From birth, both human and nonhuman primates prioritize acquisition of visual social information, orienting preferentially to faces (Deaner et al., 2005a; Heywood and Cowey, 1992)
evidence: Statement about developmental visual preferences supported by citations.

claim: Primates use the gaze direction of others as a cue to important information in the environment during development.
source: and later during development using the gaze direction of others as a cue to important information in the environment (Shepherd and Platt, 2008; Rosati et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about gaze following behavior supported by citations.

claim: Primates, including humans, selectively attend to visual cues associated with social dominance and mate quality.
source: Primates, including humans, also selectively attend to visual cues associated with social dominance and mate quality (Chance, 1967; Deaner et al., 2005b; Shepherd et al., 2006), as well as emotional states (Eastwood et al., 2001).
evidence: Statement about selective attention to social cues supported by citations.

claim: Neural circuits supporting motivation and attention are intrinsically sensitive to visual social cues to dominance.
source: Neural circuits supporting motivation and attention are intrinsically sensitive to visual social cues to dominance (Klein et al., 2009; Watson and Platt, 2012)
evidence: Statement about neural sensitivity to dominance cues supported by citations.

claim: Patterns of grooming relationships predict patterns of mutual gaze in macaques.
source: For example, patterns of grooming relationships predict patterns of mutual gaze in macaques (Ballesta and Duhamel, 2015).
evidence: Statement about relationship between grooming and gaze supported by citation.

claim: High-status monkeys selectively follow the gaze of other high-status monkeys whereas low-status monkeys follow the gaze of all monkeys.
source: Similarly, high-status monkeys selectively follow the gaze of other high-status monkeys whereas low-status monkeys follow the gaze of all monkeys (Shepherd et al., 2006).
evidence: Statement about status-dependent gaze following supported by citation.

claim: Oxytocin administration blunted the impact of social engagement on social attention.
source: Furthermore, we found that exogenous administration of the social peptide hormone oxytocin (OT) blunted the impact of social engagement on social attention.
evidence: Summary statement of oxytocin effects on SEI-attention relationship.

claim: Individual engagement in aggression within specific dyads shaped attention and OT administration increased the influence of aggressive relationships on social attention.
source: By contrast, individual engagement in aggression within specific dyads shaped attention and OT administration increased the influence of aggressive relationships on social attention.
evidence: Summary statement of findings on IEI and oxytocin effects.

claim: Abilities for recognizing and favoring in-group members, as well as kin, are thought to have evolved as adaptive strategies that maximize fitness and maintain social cohesion.
source: Consequently, abilities for recognizing and favoring in-group members, as well as kin, are thought to have evolved as adaptive strategies that maximize fitness and maintain social cohesion (Bergman et al., 2003).
evidence: Statement about evolutionary adaptation supported by citation.

claim: In-group/out-group biases can foster solidarity and cooperation within a group, but can also fuel intergroup conflict, prejudice, and discrimination.
source: Such biases foster solidarity and cooperation within a group, but can also fuel intergroup conflict, prejudice, and discrimination (Halevy et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about consequences of in-group bias supported by citation.

claim: Oxytocin is fundamental to parturition in females and is released during lactation to promote bonding between mothers and infants.
source: Oxytocin is fundamental to parturition in females and is released during lactation to promote bonding between mothers and infants.
evidence: Statement about oxytocin's reproductive functions, representing established knowledge.

claim: Oxytocin plays a crucial role in shaping social development and promoting prosocial behavior.
source: This peptide hormone also plays a crucial role in shaping social development and promoting prosocial behavior (Bauman et al., 2018; Putnam et al., 2016).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin's social functions supported by citations.

claim: Oxytocin impacts social behavior in males by influencing intra-group affinity, coordination, trust, and empathy.
source: Oxytocin also impacts social behavior in males by influencing intra-group affinity, coordination, trust, and empathy (De Dreu et al., 2011; Burkhart et al., 2022; Baumgartner et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin effects in males supported by citations.

claim: Both male and female chimpanzees have shown increased levels of oxytocin before and after intergroup conflicts.
source: Both male and female chimpanzees have shown increased levels of oxytocin before and after intergroup conflicts (Samuni et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin levels in chimpanzees supported by citation.

claim: Oxytocin enhances empathy and cooperation towards in-group conspecifics but increases competitiveness and hostility towards individuals from other groups.
source: Specifically, oxytocin enhances empathy and cooperation towards in-group conspecifics but increases competitiveness and hostility towards individuals from other groups (De Dreu and Kret, 2016; Zhang et al., 2019; Shamay-Tsoory and Abu-Akel, 2016).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin's differential effects on in-group vs out-group behavior supported by citations.

claim: Individual variation in oxytocin concentration predicts social functioning in humans.
source: These findings resonate with prior work showing that individual variation in oxytocin concentration predicts social functioning in humans (Parker et al., 2014)
evidence: Statement about oxytocin-behavior relationship in humans supported by citation.

claim: Exogenous administration of oxytocin only improves social function in children with low endogenous levels of the peptide hormone.
source: and that exogenous administration of oxytocin only improves social function in children with low endogenous levels of the peptide hormone (Parker et al., 2017).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin treatment effects supported by citation.

claim: Primate brains evolved to navigate the demands of living in a complex social environment.
source: Primate brains evolved to navigate the demands of living in a complex social environment (Dunbar and Shultz, 2007; Cheney et al., 1986).
evidence: Statement about brain evolution supported by citations.

claim: Both brain structure and function reflect social behavioral complexity.
source: A growing body of evidence indicates both brain structure and function reflect social behavioral complexity (Sallet et al., 2011; Testard et al., 2022; Sliwa and Freiwald, 2017).
evidence: Statement about brain-behavior relationships supported by citations.

claim: The 'social brain network' varies in physical size as a function of both social network size and social status.
source: For example, the so-called 'social brain network' varies in physical size as a function of both social network size and social status (Testard et al., 2022; Kanai et al., 2012; Noonan et al., 2014).
evidence: Statement about brain structure variation supported by citations.

claim: Rhesus monkeys who become more tolerant and friendly, thereby expanding their social networks, are more likely to survive natural disasters and subsequently degraded environments.
source: For example, rhesus monkeys who become more tolerant and friendly, thereby expanding their social networks, are more likely to survive natural disasters and subsequently degraded environments (Testard et al., 2024).
evidence: Statement about social behavior and survival supported by citation.

claim: Oxytocin serves as a gain control mechanism that regulates social information processing thereby shaping multi-dimensional social relationships via distinct but interacting neural pathways.
source: We further hypothesize that oxytocin serves as a gain control mechanism that regulates social information processing thereby shaping multi-dimensional social relationships via distinct but interacting neural pathways (Froemke and Young, 2021; Arakawa, 2021).
evidence: Hypothesis about oxytocin mechanism supported by citations.

claim: OT modulation of meso-cortico-limbic circuitry facilitates approach-oriented behaviors related to affiliation, familiarity, and trust, particularly towards groupmates.
source: OT modulation of meso-cortico-limbic circuitry facilitates approach-oriented behaviors related to affiliation, familiarity, and trust, particularly towards groupmates (De Dreu, 2012).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin neural mechanisms supported by citation.

claim: Oxytocin modulates cortico-amygdala circuitry, resulting in anxiolysis and reductions in fear-motivated action towards groupmates, but heightened vigilance and defensive aggression towards out-group conspecifics.
source: Oxytocin also modulates cortico-amygdala circuitry (Striepens et al., 2012), resulting in anxiolysis and reductions in fear-motivated action towards groupmates (De Dreu et al., 2015), but heightened vigilance and defensive aggression towards out-group conspecifics (De Dreu and Kret, 2016; De Dreu et al., 2015; Harari-Dahan and Bernstein, 2014).
evidence: Statement about oxytocin neural mechanisms and behavioral effects supported by multiple citations.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved in advance by the Institutional Animal Administration Committees at the Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IBP-NHP-002(22)).
source: All experimental procedures were approved in advance by the Institutional Animal Administration Committees at the Institute of Biophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences (IBP-NHP-002(22)).
evidence: Statement about ethical approval for the study.

claim: About 560 hours of video data were collected in total, monitoring interactive behaviors in each dyad among four subjects throughout the whole study.
source: We have collected about 560 hr video data totally, with monitoring interactive behaviors in each dyad among four subjects through the whole study.
evidence: Quantitative description of data collection.

claim: The most social monkey, defined by the highest SEI within the group, was equally vigilant to in-group and out-group monkeys.
source: On the other hand, the most social monkey, defined by the highest SEI within the group, was equally vigilant to in-group and out-group monkeys.
evidence: Observation about Monkey C's behavior pattern.

claim: Monkeys who were less social, as defined by lower SEIs, showed greater vigilance to out-group monkeys.
source: Monkeys who were less social, as defined by lower SEIs, showed greater vigilance to out-group monkeys.
evidence: Summary of pattern observed across subjects with different SEIs.

claim: Individual variation in sensitivity to group membership will be key for understanding the complexities of social networks in both humans and animals.
source: These findings suggest that individual variation in sensitivity to group membership will be key for understanding the complexities of social networks in both humans and animals.
evidence: Interpretation and broader implication of the findings.

claim: Variation in social information processing arises from variation in the structure and function of components of the social brain network.
source: Our study unveiled subtle variation in social information processing as a function of both general social tendencies and specific dyadic social relationships, which we hypothesize arise from variation in the structure and function of components of the social brain network.
evidence: Hypothesis connecting behavioral findings to neural mechanisms.

claim: The diverse impacts of oxytocin might be linked to many brain pathways, encompassing both the meso-cortico-limbic and cortico-amygdala circuitries.
source: The diverse impacts found here might be linked to many brain pathways, encompassing both the meso-cortico-limbic and cortico-amygdala circuitries.
evidence: Speculation about neural mechanisms underlying observed effects.

claim: The conclusions may be constrained by the relatively small sample size and the homogeneity of a stimulus set in the study.
source: However, these conclusions may be constrained by the relatively small sample size and the homogeneity of a stimulus set in the study.
evidence: Acknowledgment of study limitations.

claim: Future research focusing on larger, more diverse cohorts and incorporating a broader range of stimuli will enhance the generalizability and applicability of the findings.
source: Future research focusing on larger, more diverse cohorts and incorporating a broader range of stimuli will enhance the generalizability and applicability of the findings.
evidence: Recommendation for future research directions.
